nanguan.window: c. 1600 onward (the earliest surviving songbooks are two Ming prints; the tradition claims roots in Han to Tang music); still played by clubs in Quanzhou, Xiamen, Taiwan and the Hokkien communities of South-East Asia
nanguan.sound: The chamber music of the Minnan (Hokkien) people of southern Fujian, played in temple-linked amateur clubs: a singer beating a wooden clapper sings slow, ornate songs in Quanzhou dialect over four instruments, the pipa held horizontally, the three-string sanxian, the vertical dongxiao flute and the erxian fiddle. The repertoire runs from long instrumental zhi suites and purely instrumental pu to thousands of short sung qu.
markers: A pipa held horizontally across the lap plucks a steady, bead-like skeleton, with the sanxian under it
A piece opens on plucked strings before the dongxiao flute and erxian fiddle enter
A solo singer keeping time on the wooden clapper (paiban), singing in Quanzhou Hokkien
Very slow, gentle and heterophonic: each instrument decorates the same melody
near: Lower-Yangzi silk-and-bamboo: also amateur heterophonic chamber music, but led by erhu and dizi with an upright pipa and yangqin, purely instrumental, no Hokkien singer with clapper
Kunqu aria from The Peony Pavilion: slow, ornate qu singing like nanguan, but staged opera in Suzhou-style Mandarin over the dizi flute, not Hokkien chamber song over pipa and dongxiao
